lede: Denied a formal Latin education, he turned his outsider's status into a method: he trusted observation over authority.
copy: The illegitimate son of a Tuscan notary, Leonardo is the rare figure whose name has become shorthand for genius itself — and the reputation is earned twice over, as the painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and as a scientist and engineer who anatomised the human body, sketched flying machines and grasped principles of geology, optics and hydraulics centuries early.

What unites the painter and the investigator is relentless curiosity. His notebooks — thousands of mirror-written pages — record a mind that wanted to know how a bird's wing works, why the sky is blue, how a heart valve closes. He finished little and published nothing scientific in his lifetime, so much of his anatomical and mechanical insight died with him and had to be rediscovered.
He endures as the supreme emblem of the union of art and science: proof that the same act of careful seeing underlies a great portrait and a true theory of nature.

bio.why: Built directly from Leonardo's 7,200 surviving notebook pages, treating curiosity as the through-line of his life and work. Richly illustrated and accessible.

contested: Isaacson writes to a template — the curious outsider genius — and art historians note the book is lighter on the art-historical scholarship than on the biography. For the specialist view of Leonardo as a painter, Martin Kemp remains the standard.
